recent_posts.title: How Bending Spoons achieves 1% turnover with extreme hiring selectivity
recent_posts.summary: Bending Spoons maintains a 0.3% acceptance rate (250 hires from 800,000 applicants) using AI screening, rigorous assessments, and a 3-month cultural onboarding in Milan. They offer competitive London/New York-level salaries in Europe without bonuses or equity grants, instead allowing employees to convert compensation to discounted stock options. This approach yields 1% annual turnover compared to the industry standard of 10-20%, creating high talent density with 700 employees managing businesses averaging $50M in revenue.

recent_posts.title: How Evernote went from billion dollar startup to profitable after acquisition
recent_posts.summary: Evernote's journey from a $1 billion valuation to decline and eventual acquisition by a Milan-based company. After years of stagnation, bugs, and unprofitability, the note-taking app was acquired, underwent aggressive restructuring with a mostly European team, and returned to profitability within two years.

recent_posts.title: How bending spoons revives failing apps into billion dollar businesses
recent_posts.summary: Bending Spoons, an Italian startup valued at $11B, generates $1.5B annually by acquiring struggling but established apps like Evernote, Meetup, and WeTransfer. Their playbook: buy companies with loyal users but poor execution, send strike teams to fix bugs and optimize monetization, then hold forever rather than flip. They've completed 20 acquisitions in 10 years using proprietary tools for data analysis and decision-making, maintain 1% annual turnover with elite talent (0.003% acceptance rate), and fund growth primarily through debt rather than venture capital. The strategy focuses on improving products for paying users, raising prices, and achieving profitability through operational excellence rather than building from scratch.

recent_posts.title: How Do Kwon built and collapsed the $40 billion Terra cryptocurrency
recent_posts.summary: Do Kwon built Terra, a $40 billion cryptocurrency ecosystem featuring the UST stablecoin and LUNA token, using tactics like storytelling, community building, high returns (20%), and social proof from Wall Street and MLB sponsorships. The system collapsed in May 2022 when both tokens crashed to zero. Investigations revealed multiple lies: faked usage data, subsidized returns instead of organic revenue, missing Bitcoin reserves, prior failed attempts under a pseudonym, and market manipulation disguised as self-stabilization. Kwon was arrested in Montenegro with a fake passport, pleaded guilty to fraud and conspiracy in August 2025, and was sentenced to 15 years in prison.

recent_posts.title: The collapse of Terra Luna and Do Kwon's $40 billion cryptocurrency fraud
recent_posts.summary: Terra Luna, a $40 billion cryptocurrency project built around a stablecoin, collapsed completely within one week. The founder, Do Kwon, went on the run for nearly a year before being captured by Interpol in Montenegro. After initially pleading not guilty in January 2025, he later pleaded guilty to two fraud charges in August, admitting the project failed despite attempts to create what he called "the best currency in the world."

recent_posts.title: How Kalshi built a billion dollar prediction market using regulatory arbitrage
recent_posts.summary: Kalshi operates a federally regulated prediction market platform processing over $1 billion monthly by exploiting a legal distinction between gambling and derivatives trading. The platform enables automated trading through APIs, allowing users to build scripts that capitalize on information asymmetries like broadcast delays. The business model generates revenue from transaction fees regardless of user outcomes, while navigating complex regulatory frameworks that differentiate it from traditional gambling operations.

recent_posts.title: How Kalshi built a billion dollar prediction market using regulatory arbitrage
recent_posts.summary: Kalshi operates as a federally regulated prediction market platform processing $1B monthly by exploiting a legal loophole that classifies event contracts as commodities rather than gambling. The platform charges transaction fees (1-3.5%) instead of taking house odds, enabling users to trade yes/no contracts on events. Technical arbitrage opportunities exist through automated scripts that exploit streaming delays. After securing CFTC approval in 2020 and winning a lawsuit to enable political betting, the platform expanded into sports markets, creating regulatory tensions with states losing tax revenue.

recent_posts.title: Spotify's economic incentives are systematically replacing human artists with AI-generated music
recent_posts.summary: Spotify's business model creates perverse incentives to promote AI-generated music over human artists. The platform pays 70% of revenue to rights holders, making every major artist stream costly. This has led to alleged schemes where Spotify partners with labels to flood playlists with cheap, AI-generated background music under fake artist names. Cases like Swedish producer Johan Röhr's 15 billion streams across 650 aliases, and investigations into reduced royalty deals, suggest systematic replacement of real artists with algorithmic filler. While Spotify bans deceptive content, enforcement is inconsistent—major artists get swift protection while indie musicians face weeks-long delays removing AI impersonations. As AI music tools improve and become indistinguishable from human-created content, the platform's economic incentives point toward an ecosystem where algorithmic content dominates recommendations, potentially eroding opportunities for independent human artists.

recent_posts.title: Showrunner AI wants to disrupt Netflix with user generated content
recent_posts.summary: Showrunner AI is positioning itself as a potential Netflix disruptor by enabling users to create personalized TV shows and episodes using AI. The platform allows people to write prompts, cast characters, and generate animated content, moving beyond passive consumption to active creation. While current limitations include short animated episodes and inconsistent quality, the technology mirrors Netflix's early scrappy beginnings. The startup has already gained traction with viral AI-generated South Park episodes and has 100,000 people on their waitlist, with backing from Amazon and licensing discussions with Disney.

recent_posts.title: Tesla's camera only approach vs Waymo's lidar strategy for autonomous driving
recent_posts.summary: Tesla is pursuing a different autonomous vehicle strategy than Waymo, using only cameras and neural networks instead of expensive lidar sensors. While Waymo operates fully driverless cars in limited cities with extensive pre-mapping, Tesla deploys semi-autonomous vehicles globally to collect real-world data at scale. Tesla's approach involves liability shifting to drivers during the learning phase, allowing them to gather billions of miles of driving data. The company plans to eventually flip a software switch to convert millions of existing Teslas into fully autonomous robotaxis, creating a distributed fleet where owners can earn money from their vehicles.
